batchName: Late Republic: Marius and the Northern Invaders (121-100 BCE) - Hard Batch 1
chapterName: Late Republic: Marius and the Northern Invaders (121-100 BCE)

questions.question: Which usual rules did Marius's election as consul for 104 BC break? (select all that apply)
options: It came so soon after his first term
He stood for office while absent
He was facing a bribery trial at the time
He was under the minimum age
He was not a Roman citizen
He had never held a judicial post
questions.explanation: Standing in absence and so soon after his first term broke the usual rules, but the Assembly set them aside. Marius was still in Africa when elected.
questions.sourceQuote: Standing in absence, and so soon after his first term, broke the usual rules, but the Assembly simply set them aside.

questions.question: In what year had Marius's hometown, Arpinum, gained full Roman citizenship?
options: 218 BC
146 BC
241 BC
167 BC
188 BC
201 BC
questions.explanation: Arpinum only gained full Roman citizenship in 188 BC, about thirty years before Marius's birth. Despite local wealth, he remained an outsider in Rome.
questions.sourceQuote: His hometown had only gained full Roman citizenship in 188 BC.

questions.question: Which pieces of evidence undercut the traditional "Marian reforms" picture? (select all that apply)
options: No ancient source says he introduced cohorts
Rome abandoned conscription right after 107 BC
Late Republican armies came mostly from the cities
Citizen cavalry still appears in later evidence
Eagle standards shared the field with wolf and ox standards for decades
Archaeology shows his javelin design lasted for centuries
questions.explanation: Citizen cavalry persists, eagles shared the field with other standards, and no source credits Marius with cohorts. Archaeology suggests any javelin redesign was soon dropped, and armies still came mostly from the countryside.
questions.sourceQuote: Citizen cavalry still appears in later evidence, and eagle standards shared the field with wolf and ox standards for decades.

questions.question: What was unprecedented about the Senate's emergency decree in 100 BC?
options: It allowed troops inside the city
It was ratified by the Assembly of the plebs
It was the first ever passed by the Senate
It was the first to target serving officials rather than private citizens
It gave command to a dictator
It was proposed by a tribune
questions.explanation: For the first time, the decree targeted serving officials rather than private citizens. Marius nonetheless refused to bring an army near the city.
questions.sourceQuote: For the first time, such a decree targeted serving officials rather than private citizens.

questions.question: After the victories over the northern tribes, what controversial step did Marius take regarding Italian allied soldiers?
options: He enslaved those who had deserted
He granted citizenship to about a thousand without asking the Senate
He enrolled them all in the cavalry
He gave them all of Cisalpine Gaul
He paid them double the Roman soldiers' wages
He disbanded their units entirely
questions.explanation: Marius granted citizenship to about a thousand Italian allied soldiers without consulting the Senate. A biographer says he was hailed as Rome's "third founder", though modern historians doubt it.
questions.sourceQuote: Afterwards Marius granted citizenship to about a thousand Italian allied soldiers without asking the Senate.

questions.question: In what year did Rome, under popular pressure, finally declare war on Jugurtha?
options: 109 BC
111 BC
116 BC
113 BC
118 BC
107 BC
questions.explanation: Rome declared war in 111 BC, two years after the massacre at Cirta. The early results were humiliating, including a peace that reeked of bribery.
questions.sourceQuote: Under popular pressure, Rome declared war in 111 BC.

questions.question: Why do historians see the transfer of the African command to Marius in 107 BC as a turning point?
options: It made the consulship open to non-citizens
It abolished the tribunes' veto
It ended the Senate's right to declare war
Using popular votes to overrule the Senate on commands became a habit
It created the first permanent provincial governorship
It was the first time a novus homo held any command
questions.explanation: Overruling the Senate on military commands by popular vote became a habit copied by later generals. This fuelled bitter personal rivalries.
questions.sourceQuote: Using popular votes to overrule the Senate on military commands became a habit, and ambitious generals after Marius copied it, fuelling bitter personal rivalries.

questions.question: What did Sulla do that an ancient biographer linked to "the first seed" of his hatred with Marius?
options: He testified against Marius for bribery
He refused to march in Marius's triumph
He executed Jugurtha without orders
He stole the spoils of Capsa
He wore a ring showing Jugurtha's capture
He married Metellus's daughter
questions.explanation: Sulla wore a ring depicting the capture, and the quarrel over credit was called "the first seed" of their hatred. Jugurtha was paraded in Marius's triumph in 104 BC.
questions.sourceQuote: But Sulla wore a ring showing the capture, and an ancient biographer called the quarrel over credit "the first seed" of their hatred.

questions.question: Which Celtic tribe, allied to the Cimbri, destroyed a Roman army and killed a consul in 107 BC?
options: The Tigurini
The Allobroges
The Ambrones
The Boii
The Arverni
The Helvetii
questions.explanation: The Tigurini, a Celtic tribe allied to the Cimbri, destroyed a Roman army in 107 BC. Two years later came the catastrophe at Arausio.
questions.sourceQuote: In 107 BC their allies the Tigurini, a Celtic tribe, destroyed another army and killed a consul.

questions.question: Which actions did Marius take during the Battle of the Muthul? (select all that apply)
options: Gathered several scattered detachments
Withdrew to the river to secure the water
Led a column of about 2,000 men through the enemy
Stormed a desert fortress after a forty-day siege
Captured Jugurtha's royal standard
Helped seize a hill held by Numidian infantry
questions.explanation: Marius gathered scattered units, led about 2,000 men through the enemy to Metellus, and helped seize a hill before striking the cavalry from behind. The forty-day siege of a desert fortress came later, under Metellus.
questions.sourceQuote: He gathered several scattered detachments and led a column of about 2,000 men through the enemy to link up with Metellus.
